lesson.text: Quick memory: last unit, forecasting hazards. What data warns a town of a coming flood? Rainfall and rising river levels.
People change the environment when they build, farm, travel and make things. As the number of people grows, so does our impact: about 1 billion people in 1800, about 8 billion today.
Harmful impacts include pollution, cutting down forests, overfishing, and plastic in the oceans.
Engineers and communities design solutions: cleaner energy, recycling, protected areas, fishing limits and plastic-free choices.
A good solution is tested: does it work, how much does it cost, and does it cause new problems?
Try it in the world: design a greener town in your world: a bus stop, bike paths, solar panels on the roofs and a park. What problem does each one fix? Next: engineering design.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a harmful impact on the environment?
exercises.explain: Plastic in the ocean harms sea life.

exercises.prompt: Which one helps reduce plastic waste?
exercises.hint: Which choice means using something again instead of throwing it away?
exercises.explain: Reusable bottles mean less plastic thrown away.

exercises.prompt: As more people live on Earth, our impact on the environment can grow.
exercises.explain: Yes: more people means more building, farming and travel.

exercises.prompt: What is overfishing?
exercises.hint: Think of a sea where fishing boats take fish faster than new fish hatch.
choices: catching fish faster than they can breed
exercises.explain: Overfishing takes fish faster than they can be replaced.

exercises.prompt: Recycling paper saves trees.
exercises.explain: Yes: recycled paper means fewer trees cut down.

exercises.prompt: Why do fishing limits help?
exercises.hint: If fewer fish are caught, what can the others do?
exercises.explain: Fewer fish caught gives them time to breed.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a protected area?
exercises.explain: National parks protect habitats.

exercises.prompt: A town wants cleaner air. Which idea helps most?
exercises.hint: Which choice makes no smoke or fumes in the town?
exercises.explain: Electric buses give off no exhaust fumes in the town.

exercises.prompt: Cutting down forests can harm the animals that live there.
exercises.explain: Yes: they lose their habitat.

exercises.prompt: What should engineers test about a solution?
choices: whether it works and what it costs
exercises.explain: They test how well it works and its cost.

exercises.prompt: A dam gives clean energy but floods a valley. What does this show?
choices: A solution can cause new problems.
exercises.explain: Solutions have trade-offs that must be weighed.

exercises.prompt: One litter bin costs more but gets used more. How should the town choose?
choices: Weigh cost against how well it works.
exercises.explain: A good choice weighs cost against results.

exercises.prompt: Every solution to an environmental problem is perfect.
exercises.explain: No: solutions have costs and can cause new problems.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps of designing a solution.
exercises.explain: Find the problem, think of ideas, build and test, then improve.

exercises.prompt: Which change would lower a family's impact the most over a year?
choices: walking or cycling instead of short drives
exercises.explain: Replacing many short car trips saves the most fuel.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to a solution.
exercises.hint: Ask what each solution stops or puts back.
exercises.explain: Overfishing: fishing limits. Plastic waste: reusable bottles. Lost forests: replanting and reserves. Smoky air: electric buses.

exercises.prompt: Sort the impacts: harmful or helpful to the environment?
exercises.hint: Does it damage habitats and resources, or protect them?
exercises.explain: Plastic in the ocean, overfishing and cutting forests harm. A reserve, recycling paper and fishing limits help.

exercises.prompt: Sort the solutions by the problem they help with.
exercises.hint: Ask what each one stops: fumes, plastic, or trees being lost?
exercises.explain: Dirty air: electric buses and cycling cut exhaust fumes. Plastic waste: reusable bottles and paper straws. Lost forests: replanting trees and nature reserves.

exercises.prompt: There were about 1 billion people on Earth in 1800 and there are about 8 billion today. How many times as many people is that?
exercises.hint: Divide today's number of people by the number in 1800.
exercises.explain: 8 billion ÷ 1 billion: 8 times as many people. That means far more building, farming and travel, so our impact has grown too.

exercises.prompt: A town tries a new recycling scheme. Sort the questions: a good test of the solution, or not?
items: Is the bin a nice colour?
exercises.hint: Card 4: does it work, what does it cost, and does it cause new problems?
exercises.explain: Good tests ask whether it works (less rubbish, people using it), what it costs, and whether it causes new problems. The bin's colour tells you nothing about the solution.
